incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, reports that scammers are using artificial intelligence to create fake videos and social media profiles impersonating him. The criminals use AI-generated images and videos to offer immigration services Leal never provides, targeting vulnerable immigrants seeking legal help. Scammers request payments of thousands of dollars, including a $2,200 fee for fake US residency assistance. Leal first discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, though suspicious activity began last October and has escalated dramatically over the past three months.

His firm hired an anti-piracy company that has removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The scams typically start with social media videos directing viewers to contact a WhatsApp number, where fraudsters send fake contracts and request payment through digital apps like Venmo and Zelle. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate. He advises immigrants seeking legal services online to verify identities and avoid anyone requesting immediate payment through social media.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake online article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock engaged in a heated confrontation represents a growing type of scam using artificial intelligence. The fabricated interview promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, and never actually occurred. This scheme exemplifies how scammers increasingly use AI-generated deepfakes and convincing fake content to deceive investors, making fraudulent opportunities appear legitimate and trustworthy.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission data reveals these investment scams are becoming more prevalent and sophisticated. Last year, the regulator removed 19,400 scams overall, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated figures. ASIC warns consumers to verify financial services licenses independently through official registers and advises that familiar branding or polished content does not guarantee legitimacy. Kohler has called for heavy fines against platforms and AI models that enable these scams.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco accuses Oura, a smart ring company valued at $11 billion, of false advertising regarding its sleep tracking capabilities. The suit claims that Oura's rings, which cost $300 and up, cannot accurately measure different sleep stages as the company advertises. Instead of detecting actual physiological signals like a hospital sleep lab would, the lawsuit alleges Oura's devices rely on AI-generated estimates that are no more reliable than a coin flip. Oura markets its rings as having 95% sleep staging accuracy compared to clinical sleep labs, but the lawsuit points out that real sleep labs use complex methods with multiple electrodes to measure brain activity, which Oura's wearables lack.

Oura responded by standing behind its research and accuracy claims, stating that its rings use multiple physiological signals and have been validated against polysomnography in peer-reviewed studies. The company emphasized that while Oura Ring is not a medical device or substitute for clinical sleep studies, it provides useful estimates. It remains unclear what compensation customers could receive if the lawsuit succeeds. This is not Oura's first legal challenge, as the company also faces an ongoing class-action suit alleging it collected personal information without customer consent over a two-year period.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's threat intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group has been actively targeting ESXi environments since April 2026. The group developed a Linux variant of their ransomware that encrypts virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. Between April and May 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks across ten target organizations. The agent assisted with various tasks including network scanning, privilege enumeration, and authentication attacks, though many commands initially failed and required refinement.

In a separate discovery, researchers identified a second Aurora cluster operating across eight victim organizations in multiple countries. This cluster used different tactics, including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. The investigation revealed multiple infrastructure indicators including command and control servers, proxy IPs, and the group's onion-based victim negotiation portal. Gambit Security published these technical details and indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and defend against Aurora ransomware campaigns.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
A Pizza Hut franchisee filed a lawsuit in Texas claiming that Pizza Hut's mandatory adoption of Dragontail, an AI-powered delivery management system, caused over $100 million in damages. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates 111 restaurants across the Northeast, alleges the system created operational failures after its 2024 rollout. The platform gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen operations, causing drivers to wait up to 15 minutes to batch multiple orders together rather than delivering pizzas immediately, which slowed service and disappointed customers. The franchisee also claims drivers could see tip amounts and payment methods, making them selective about which orders to accept.

Before the rollout, Chaac maintained over 90 percent on-time delivery rates and double-digit sales growth, but after implementing Dragontail, performance deteriorated significantly. In New York City specifically, year-over-year sales swung from positive 10.19 percent to negative 9.78 percent. The suit claims Pizza Hut failed to provide adequate training, ignored support requests, and breached the franchise agreement by mandating continued use of the faulty system. Pizza Hut stated it would respond through legal channels but declined further comment.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
Scammers have been sending personalized emails to authors, entertainers, and public figures impersonating Terry Gross, the host of NPR's "Fresh Air," to lure them into a fraud scheme. The emails reference the recipient's work and propose interview topics, making them appear legitimate. Eventually, the scammers request payment, typically around $250, claiming it covers production costs. WHYY, NPR, and the "Fresh Air" production team have confirmed they never charge guests for interviews and are investigating the matter with law enforcement.

Cybersecurity experts say artificial intelligence has made these impersonation scams more convincing and personalized than previous fraud attempts. Red flags include emails from suspicious addresses like "terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com," requests for payment, and the unusually personal involvement of Gross herself in logistics. Potential victims should verify suspicious requests by contacting the organization directly through legitimate channels rather than responding to the email. Experts warn that as AI technology improves, such sophisticated scams targeting well-known individuals will likely become increasingly common.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Israeli-funded operatives created a fake American thinktank called the Hanover Institute to influence artificial intelligence systems toward pro-Israel messaging. The nonexistent organization published 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words in nine days, designed to appear in chatbot responses when users search for information about topics like Israeli war crimes and Gaza casualties. The website was built on a platform specifically optimized to make AI systems cite its content, and it framed controversial issues in ways that consistently favored Israel's position while citing legitimate sources to appear credible.

The operation is part of a broader Israeli government campaign financed through tens of millions of dollars routed via international advertising firms, with contracts worth tens of millions awarded without competitive bidding. Israeli officials have reportedly expressed frustration that the expensive public diplomacy efforts have failed to improve Israel's standing in American public opinion, which has shifted significantly against Israel since 2022. Researchers warn that this strategy represents a new threat where foreign governments can manipulate AI training data in ways that voters cannot easily fact-check.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse both companies of scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and of directly reproducing sections of famous recordings. The lawsuits involve music from artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Mariah Carey, and Bruce Springsteen. The record labels claim both companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data and refused to disclose which songs were used.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate famous songs by using specific prompts describing the original music's style, genre, and era. They provided examples showing how prompts like "1954 rock and roll billy haley comets" generated outputs mimicking original songs, and how requesting "Mariah Carey contemporary r&b holiday" produced near-identical versions of "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The record labels submitted a thumbdrive of these AI-generated songs as evidence. Udio was sued in New York while Suno was sued in Massachusetts, setting up major legal battles over how generative AI services handle copyrighted material.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers apologized after using artificial intelligence to prepare legal filings in a lawsuit brought by Los Angeles homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga. The homeowner's attorneys discovered that the State Farm filings contained fabricated case citations, fake quotes, and non-existent legal holdings. Meni-Siliga sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire made her Carson home uninhabitable, followed by water damage during repairs. She claimed delays in getting State Farm's approval prevented completion of reconstruction work, leading her and her husband to exhaust their savings, declare bankruptcy, and lose their home to foreclosure.

Attorney Jacquelene Robinson acknowledged using an AI tool called Irys to prepare the motions, mistakenly believing it performed accuracy checks. She confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and quotes. State Farm's lead counsel accepted responsibility for the errors. The case is scheduled for trial in October. This incident reflects a growing trend, with 41 percent of law firms now using generative AI, though a Paris-based database has documented nearly 1,922 legal hallucination cases worldwide, primarily in the United States.

stories.Headline: China promotes coordinated development of data industry, artificial intelligence-- Beijing Review
stories.Summary:
# Summary

China's data industry reached 6.78 trillion yuan in 2025, and the country is now focusing on coordinating development between its data sector and artificial intelligence capabilities. The 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo, held in Guiyang from August 28-30, attracted 372 companies and over 16,000 guests to showcase innovations in computing power, large models, and data circulation. Government officials emphasized that high-quality datasets are essential for advancing AI capabilities and that data technology is transforming traditional industries like power generation and renewable energy forecasting.

Beyond upgrading existing industries, data and AI are creating new business opportunities and employment categories. Companies are hiring data collectors to train robots through embodied intelligence projects, while micro-enterprises and one-person startups are emerging as signs of entrepreneurial growth. International participants from Zimbabwe, Chile, Pakistan, and other nations attended to explore cooperation opportunities, with officials highlighting the potential for shared benefits and technological exchange between countries through collaborative data and AI development.

stories.Headline: EU places ChatGPT, Reddit, Roblox under strictest platform rules
stories.Summary:
The European Union has classified ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine and designated Reddit and Roblox as Very Large Online Platforms under its Digital Services Act. These three American companies will now face direct supervision from the European Commission and must comply with stricter requirements designed to address risks related to children, election integrity, and public security. The rules apply to services with over 45 million users in the EU, bringing the total number of regulated platforms to 28.

Companies failing to meet the new requirements within four months face fines up to 6 percent of their annual global revenue. Reddit reported 57.2 million EU users in July, while Roblox has 46.6 million. OpenAI stated it would prepare to meet ChatGPT's additional obligations, and Roblox welcomed the designation, emphasizing safety's importance. This designation adds another regulatory layer for ChatGPT, which already complies with the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act.

Taiwan is focusing on developing sovereign AI systems that understand Taiwanese perspectives and languages, along with low-Earth-orbit satellite communications to ensure independent communication capabilities. Officials emphasized that technological sovereignty means focusing on critical technologies rather than developing every technology domestically.

stories.Headline: Who Writes AI's Rules When Someone Else Owns the Machines?
stories.Summary:
# Summary

South Africa withdrew its Draft National AI Policy in April 2026 after discovering that at least six of its 67 academic references were fabricated, highlighting a broader challenge facing the Global South. The incident underscores a critical debate about who controls artificial intelligence governance and infrastructure. Currently, the United States and China host roughly 86% of global data centre capacity, giving them power to set rules and prices for AI systems worldwide. This concentration of computing power represents what critics call "tech colonialism," where developing nations provide data and demand but lack ownership and control over the technology itself.

BRICS countries and other Global South nations are attempting to shift AI governance away from Western-led standards by emphasizing digital sovereignty and development rights. They are seeking to anchor AI governance within the United Nations rather than OECD-led bodies and have established organizations like the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. However, meaningful sovereignty requires owning physical infrastructure, not just adopting policies. The article notes that until developing nations build regional computing capacity and chip manufacturing capabilities, they remain dependent on foreign platforms controlled by American hyperscalers or Chinese firms. True sovereignty means choosing dependencies rather than having them imposed.

stories.Headline: CSA's Top Cloud Threats: Identity, AI -- Campus Technology
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Security Alliance surveyed 507 security professionals to identify the top threats to cloud computing in 2026. Identity and access management issues rose to the number one concern, moving up from second place in 2024, while misconfiguration dropped to fifth. Two artificial intelligence-related threats appeared in the rankings for the first time, including AI-enhanced attacks and AI system compromise. The top eleven threats also include insecure third-party resources, insecure APIs, advanced persistent threats, and inadequate cloud security strategy and governance.

The survey results reveal a significant shift in the cloud threat landscape, with organizations now prioritizing identity protection, artificial intelligence risks, and software supply chains over infrastructure-focused concerns. Security scores ranged closely from 7.95 for identity and access management to 7.45 for system vulnerabilities. The report aims to help organizations make informed risk-management decisions about cloud adoption by providing expert analysis of technical and business impacts, real-world examples, and corresponding security controls across cloud and AI environments.

The article argues that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, not Nvidia or AMD, will be the ultimate winner in the artificial intelligence hardware race. While many investors focus on chip designers like Nvidia and AMD, the author contends that Taiwan Semiconductor holds the real advantage because it manufactures chips for these companies and controls approximately 72 percent of the global foundry market. Since Nvidia and AMD do not build their own chips, they must rely on Taiwan Semiconductor's manufacturing capacity.

Taiwan Semiconductor benefits from a neutral position in the competition between chip designers, meaning it will profit regardless of which company's hardware becomes dominant. The company's CEO expects elevated demand for chips to continue through at least 2029 or 2030, providing several more years of strong growth. Additionally, Taiwan Semiconductor plans to launch new chip technology that will allow for price increases, positioning it as one of the safest investments in the artificial intelligence sector.
